Luxury cars can differ massively from one another, but most of us make similar assumptions when describing the term "luxury car." We picture leather seats, 20-plus-inch chrome wheels, full-size silhouettes, and big displacement engines with a lot of cylinders . However, every once in a while, automakers mix things up a little and throw in an ingredient you might not expect. Four-cylinder engines are one such ingredient, and they found themselves in luxury cars from an assortment of automakers, spanning across what is almost the entire history of the automobile so far.

We're talking Fiats from the turn of the 20th century, British executive sedans produced by Rover in the late '60s and early '70s, hybridized BMW 5 Series sedans, Range Rover SUVs, and more. What's interesting here is that, for the most part, all of these cars were and are considered successes, with rare exceptions (Facel Vega Facellia, we're looking at you), which suggests luxury car buyers aren't actually all that hung up on the engine under the hood. Without further ado, here are our seven four-cylinder luxury cars, in chronological order.

But can a single tire really handle every single situation well? Our friends at Tyre Reviews compared eight of them to find out.

The newest tire in the comparison is the Continental SecureContact AW, and when it comes to premium tires, a lot of times the newest one is the best. But is that the case here? Well, Tyre Reviews put it up against Michelin's legendary CrossClimate2, the Goodyear Assurance WeatherReady 2, Bridgestone's WeatherPeak, the Pirelli Cinturato WeatherActive, the Hankook Weatherflex GT, the Falken Aklimate, and the Atturo AZ810. Sometimes, people will give serious things unserious names. A velvet ant, for example, may sound like a tiny critter that's covered in the sort of material you'd find in an old Land Rover's interior, but it actually has one of the most painful stings in the animal kingdom. Then there's the panhandle hooker: though it sounds like a questionably frisky profession, it actually refers to a dangerous storm that develops in the panhandles of Texas and Oklahoma.

Or how about the Phantom Badger? We'd have thought it was a mischievous weasel that has a mask-like face, but no. It's actually the name of a military vehicle that was built by Boeing, in partnership with MSI Defense Solutions, starting in 2013. The Phantom Badger was designed to assist U.S. Marine and Air Force squads with a variety of tasks, including, but not limited to, casualty evacuation, reconnaissance missions, and search and rescue.

The Chevrolet Corvette has been Detroit's answer to the European sports car for more than seventy years. Since 1953, it has gone through eight distinct generations. The idea behind the Corvette came from Harley Earl, former head of design at General Motors, who envisioned an affordable two-seat roadster that could stand beside the imports returning stateside with World War II veterans. The first Corvette shipped with a six-cylinder engine, and it was Zora Arkus-Duntov (later nicknamed the " Father of the Corvette ") who pushed the car towards the V8 power it would become known for.

From there, the Corvette never stopped evolving. The front-engine layout that defined the nameplate for decades was finally abandoned when the eighth generation arrived with its engine behind the driver, a change that purists argued about — and the stopwatch quietly settled. What makes the Corvette so interesting is that it has always been judged by two audiences. One cares about straight-line muscle and badge pride. The other, which is usually more critical, cares about how a car handles when the road bends. And for a car built to take on Porsche, Jaguar, and Ferrari, that second audience matters just as much as the first — if not more.

Heading into the 1960s, Detroit's Big Three had begun to realize some folks preferred cars that were more agile and more efficient than the typically massive machines they were producing. Their response was to introduce a wave of home-grown compacts in 1960, led by GM's Chevrolet Corvair, the Chrysler Valiant, and the Ford Falcon.

On the truck side of the ledger, though, things played out differently. Datsun had been exporting compact trucks to the West Coast since the first half of the 1960s, with Toyota following soon after. The Big Three at the time offered car-based trucks like the Corvair forward-control models and the Falcon-based ute-style Ranchero, but they didn't look like the real deal the way the Japanese mini-trucks did. So when the mini-truck segment began taking off, the U.S. automakers went straight to the easiest option. Ford rebadged Mazda's B-series truck to sell as the Courier for 1972. The same year saw GM give that treatment to the Isuzu Faster, with the result being the Chevy LUV — a truck way ahead of its time .

item.title: What The 'E' On A Manual Gear Shift Means (And When To Use It)
item.dc:creator: Marco Rossi
item.description: Long before our cars got fancy drive mode selectors, trick cylinder deactivation tech, and varying levels of hybrid assistance , automakers had to get creative with their engineering approach to satisfy the tightening fuel economy standards that arrived during the oil crisis of the late '70s and early '80s.

Long before our cars got fancy drive mode selectors, trick cylinder deactivation tech, and varying levels of hybrid assistance , automakers had to get creative with their engineering approach to satisfy the tightening fuel economy standards that arrived during the oil crisis of the late '70s and early '80s. Volkswagen's solution was a special manual gearbox design where the final shift gate was marked with a capital 'E'.

The '3+E' and '4+E' setups found in the original VW Golf , Jetta, and the U.S.-spec Rabbit models had nothing to do with electrification. Many drivers at the time understandably assumed that the letter stood for 'Economy' or an 'Extra' gear. However, Volkswagen documents confirm that the magic word is 'Efficiency'. Rather than being a new designation for the fourth or fifth gears, the 'E' slot engaged an overdrive designed to lower engine speeds, minimize wear, and improve the fuel economy ratings at highway speeds.

Cars are dangerous. There's no shortage of studies reiterating that fact, from the frequent running down of pedestrians over the last century to the not-so-obvious deaths outside of traffic crashes . It's why many of today's cars are inundated with those darn safety features we'd sacrifice if given the option. And yet another danger lurks in an unexpected place: the closet. Caution the fashionistas in your life, because your car and a scarf could be a deadly combination.

Death by scarf via the automobile became a phenomenon nearly 100 years ago, when in 1927, famous American dancer Isadora Duncan met her tragic end from the combination of the two in France. The New York Times wrote that on the night of the accident, she wore an "immense iridescent silk scarf wrapped about her neck and streaming in long folds, part of which was swathed about her body with part trailing behind."

With national diesel prices inching towards $7/gallon and Tesla’s $290,000 Semi trucks finally making their way to paying customers , it’s worth revisiting how Trump’s One Big, Beautiful Bill Act (OBBA) helped beef up the Section 179 deduction, and look again at how it could help your fleet ditch diesel sooner rather than later.

At the core of this thinking is the fact that the IRS does not distinguish between fuel choices, so there’s no separate depreciation category for electric- vs. diesel-fueled commercial trucks. The relevant classifications, then, are the vehicle’s use and property classes, and under the IRS’ depreciation guidelines, tractor units designed for over-the-road use are classified as 3-year properties and fall under the 20-year recovery threshold for 100% bonus depreciation, Tesla’s electric Semi can benefit from 179 just like their diesel-powered competitors. But don’t get me wrong – this isn’t just great news for Tesla Semi buyers. Electric garbage trucks , electric vocational trucks , battery electric reefer trailers , and even some big electric forklifts can potentially benefit from the same accelerated depreciation rules, since the IRS lists these as, “specialized business vehicles,” with no distinction between electric, diesel, natural gas, hydrogen , magic pixie dust, anything else.

Was a Corvette more affordable in real terms in 2007, for example, than a 2027 model is today? We dug through old price lists and discovered that, while the 2007 C6 Vette initially appears to be almost half the price of a new C8, the pair cost near identical amounts when inflation is taken into account.

The sixth-generation C6 Corvette debuted at the Detroit Auto Show in January 2004, and went into production that summer as a 2005 model, in coupe and convertible form. Both came with a new 6.0L LS2 V8 that made 400 horsepower. Yet looking at the actual numbers, the 911 and the ZR1 are both quicker than the aforementioned supercar and hypercar, which makes no sense.

The Lamborghini Miura is often credited as the car that popularized the term "supercar," but the word itself existed long before the Miura . If you don't care to participate, you can use apps like MapQuest to avoid these cameras , or FlockHopper to automatically route around them. Or you can do as YouTuber Studio Hotrods did, and design a system to make your license plate invisible, but only near a Flock camera.

What Studio Hotrods came up with is a clever system that obscures your plate only when you're in view of a Flock camera. The video goes into detail, but basically, an Arduino computer controls a piece of smart glass that's clear when it receives power but turns opaque when the power shuts off.
